![](../../img/conversation_2780E3.svg){.page-art}

*An in-class activity. Nothing to turn in and no answer key -- this one needs
other people, which is why it happens in class rather than at home.*

**The idea.** Almost nothing on the questionable-practices list is wrong in
itself. What makes an act a problem is when it was decided and whether it was
disclosed -- and the only way to feel that is to try to separate two people who
wrote identical methods sections.

**Format.** About 12 minutes · threes · no laptop needed.

## 1. Your pair (2 minutes)

Each group takes **one** pair. Both researchers did the same thing.

> **Pair 1.** (i) Rania excludes 6 participants for failing an attention check she
> defined before collecting data. (ii) Sam excludes 6 for failing an attention
> check, after noticing it moves his effect below .05.

> **Pair 2.** (i) Jae collects 50, finds nothing, and collects 30 more because
> the grant year is ending. (ii) Mira collects 50, sees $p = .07$, and collects
> 30 more.

> **Pair 3.** (i) Dev log-transforms a skewed outcome, as his lab always does
> with reaction times. (ii) Wren tries raw, log, and rank, and reports the log.

> **Pair 4.** (i) Tomás reports an unexpected age effect as exploratory.
> (ii) Priya introduces the same unexpected age effect in her introduction as the
> study's hypothesis.

## 2. Try to separate them (6 minutes)

- Write the sentence in the methods section that would differ between (i) and
  (ii). If none would, say so -- that is an allowed answer.
- Is the *statistical* damage the same in both halves? Is the *ethical* judgment?
- What single published fact would let a reader tell them apart?
- One of your two is something most researchers have done. Which, and at what
  exact moment did it become questionable?

## 3. Report out (4 minutes)

Each group gives its pair in thirty seconds: **separable or not**, and by what.

- How many pairs did the room find separable from the published record alone?
- Given that answer, what follows for how you read other people's papers -- and
  for how you work yourself?

*If you have more time: who benefits from each practice, past the researcher --
the lab, the journal, the field? And why does the file drawer survive when
nobody is ever accused of it?*

{{< dstart summary="If you were not in class" >}}

Almost no group can separate their pair. The methods sections are identical or
near enough: same exclusions, same final $n$, same transformation, same reported
effect. What differs is when the decision was made and what it was made in
response to -- information that exists only in the researcher's head, which is
the entire argument for writing it down in advance.

The statistical damage is *not* symmetric. Rania's rule is independent of the
results, so her stated error rate holds. Sam's is conditional on the data, so his
real false-positive rate exceeds .05 by an amount neither he nor his reader can
compute. Same six participants, same table, different evidence.

Pair 2 splits rooms and should. Jae and Mira end up with identical datasets.
Mira's stopping rule is a function of the $p$-value, which inflates her effect
and her error rate; Jae's is a function of the grant calendar, which is unrelated
to the result. This is why "we collected more data" is not itself an accusation,
and also why "we had leftover money" is not a defence anyone can verify.

Two consequences worth sitting with. You usually cannot detect this in someone
else's paper, which is why the field moved toward preregistration rather than
toward better reviewing. And less comfortably: you cannot reliably detect it in
yourself, because the reasoning feels principled at the time.
